name: Peter
reliabilityNote: Multiple early sources: 1 Clement (c. 96), Origen, Eusebius.
scripture: A fisherman of Bethsaida, called with his brother Andrew: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:18–20). Jesus renamed him Peter — “rock” — and promised, “on this rock I will build my church,” giving him the keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:18–19). He denied Christ three times, was restored with “feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17), and preached the Pentecost sermon that brought three thousand into the Church (Acts 2).
tradition: Peter led the Church at Jerusalem, then traveled to Rome, where he was martyred under Nero (c. 64–67) — crucified upside down, deeming himself unworthy to die as his Lord did. His tomb is venerated beneath St. Peter’s Basilica.

name: James, son of Zebedee
reliabilityNote: His martyrdom is recorded in Scripture itself.
scripture: A Galilean fisherman called with his brother John, nicknamed “Sons of Thunder” for their zeal (Mark 3:17). He belonged to Jesus’s inner circle — present at the Transfiguration and in Gethsemane. He was the first apostle martyred: beheaded by Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:2).
tradition: A much later medieval legend made James the evangelizer of Spain, and his shrine at Santiago de Compostela became one of Christendom’s great pilgrimages. The Spain connection is pious legend, not early tradition.

name: John
reliabilityNote: Irenaeus (a disciple of John’s own disciple Polycarp) and Eusebius.
scripture: Son of Zebedee and “Son of Thunder,” he reclined at Jesus’s breast at the Last Supper (John 13:23) and was entrusted with Mary at the cross: “Behold, your mother” (John 19:26–27). Tradition ascribes to him the fourth Gospel, three epistles, and Revelation, written in exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9).
tradition: John ministered at Ephesus, survived exile under Domitian, and died of old age there — the only apostle not martyred.

name: Andrew
reliabilityNote: The Greek mission is ancient; the X-shaped cross comes from later accounts.
scripture: Peter’s brother, a fisherman first discipled by John the Baptist. Hearing “Behold, the Lamb of God,” he followed Jesus and brought Peter to him (John 1:40–42) — the first evangelist. He later brought the boy with loaves and fishes to Jesus (John 6:8–9).
tradition: Andrew is said to have preached in Greece and Scythia, and to have been crucified at Patras on an X-shaped cross — the “St. Andrew’s cross” of Scotland’s flag, where his relics were long claimed.

name: Philip
reliabilityNote: Eusebius and Polycrates (2nd century) place him at Hierapolis.
scripture: From Bethsaida, called directly by Jesus: “Follow me” (John 1:43). He brought Nathanael with the words “Come and see” (John 1:46), calculated the cost of feeding the five thousand (John 6:7), and asked at the Last Supper, “Lord, show us the Father” (John 14:8).
tradition: Early sources place Philip’s ministry and martyrdom at Hierapolis in Phrygia (modern Turkey), where he is said to have been crucified — not to be confused with Philip the Evangelist of Acts.

name: Bartholomew
reliabilityNote: Early sources agree he went east; the manner of his death is disputed among late accounts.
scripture: Named in every apostolic list but never described there; John’s Gospel never names Bartholomew but presents Nathanael — brought by Philip, greeted by Jesus as “an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47). Since the lists pair Bartholomew with Philip, the Church has long read them as one man.
tradition: Eusebius records that Bartholomew preached in India, leaving a Hebrew copy of Matthew’s Gospel found there a century later. Later accounts send him to Armenia, where he was martyred — by crucifixion, beheading, or (in the famous 9th-century Armenian telling) flayed alive, which is why art shows him holding his own skin, as in the Sistine Chapel.

name: Matthew
reliabilityNote: His Gospel and calling are certain; his later field is reported variously.
scripture: A tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, despised by his own people — called straight from his booth: “Follow me. And he rose and followed him” (Matthew 9:9). He hosted a banquet for Jesus attended by fellow outcasts, and tradition names him author of the first Gospel, written for Jewish Christians.
tradition: Accounts of Matthew’s later ministry scatter him across Ethiopia, Persia, and Judea, and his martyrdom is reported variously — a reminder of how thin the record grows for the quieter apostles.

name: Thomas
reliabilityNote: The 3rd-century Acts of Thomas plus an unbroken living community in Kerala.
scripture: Famously “doubting Thomas” — he refused to believe without touching the wounds (John 20:25), then made the highest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). But he had also been the brave one: “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16).
tradition: Thomas is said to have sailed to India, landing in 52 AD at Muziris on the Malabar Coast, founding seven churches in Kerala. The St. Thomas Christians there trace their lineage to him to this day; tradition holds he was speared to death near Mylapore (Chennai) around 72 AD.

name: James, son of Alphaeus
reliabilityNote: Scripture names him and little more; later reports conflict.
scripture: Named in every apostolic list, and almost nowhere else — possibly the “James the younger” at the cross (Mark 15:40). His obscurity is itself a lesson: most of the Twelve served and died without the record-keeping we wish we had.
tradition: Later accounts variously send him to Jerusalem, Egypt, or Persia, with conflicting reports of his martyrdom. Honesty requires admitting how little survives.

name: Jude Thaddaeus
reliabilityNote: The identification of the names is traditional; the eastern mission is late.
scripture: Listed as “Judas son of James” by Luke and “Thaddaeus” by Matthew and Mark — the Church reads them as one man. At the Last Supper he asked the question every believer has asked: “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?” (John 14:22). Tradition names him author of the Epistle of Jude.
tradition: Jude is said to have preached in Persia and Armenia alongside Simon the Zealot, and to have been martyred there. His patronage of hopeless causes comes from the faithful’s reluctance to pray to anyone named Judas — so those who did, and were heard, told everyone.

alsoKnownAs: Simon the Zealot; Simon the Cananaean
name: Simon
reliabilityNote: Everything beyond his name and title comes from late, conflicting reports.
scripture: Named in every list with the title “the Zealot” (Luke 6:15) — whether a former member of the nationalist party or simply a man of zeal, he is proof that Christ’s circle held opposites together: a Zealot beside Matthew the tax-collector collaborator.
tradition: Tradition pairs Simon with Jude in Persia, where both were reportedly martyred — one late account says Simon was sawn in half. The details are legend; the mission east is the consistent thread.

name: Matthias
reliabilityNote: Acts records his election; everything after is various and late.
scripture: Not one of the original Twelve, but the Church’s first act after the Ascension was to restore their number: Matthias, who had followed Jesus “from the baptism of John,” was chosen by lot to take Judas’s place (Acts 1:21–26) — the last decision ever made that way.
tradition: Later accounts scatter Matthias to Ethiopia, Judea, or the Caspian region, with conflicting martyrdom reports. He is the patron of alcoholics and of perseverance — the man called to fill the hardest vacancy in history.

name: Paul
reliabilityNote: His letters are firsthand; his Roman martyrdom is reported by 1 Clement (c. 96) and Eusebius.
scripture: A Pharisee who hunted Christians until Christ struck him down on the Damascus road (Acts 9:3–6). Baptized, he became the tireless missionary of three great journeys, founder of churches across the empire, and author of thirteen New Testament letters — the deepest theological mind of the apostolic age.
tradition: Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero (c. 64–67) — as a Roman citizen, spared crucifixion. His tomb is venerated at St. Paul Outside the Walls. With Peter, he is co-patron of Rome and of the Church’s mission to the world.

feast: None — he is commemorated, not celebrated
name: Judas Iscariot
reliabilityNote: Both Gospel accounts agree on the betrayal and the remorse; they differ on the manner of death.
scripture: The Twelve’s treasurer, who sold Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14–16). When remorse came, he returned the silver — “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” — and despaired instead of repenting (Matthew 27:3–5). Matthew records that he hanged himself; Acts describes his death in the Field of Blood (Acts 1:18–19). He is included here for completeness: the Church does not edit its wounds out of the story.
tradition: The early Church’s verdict is sober, not vindictive: Judas shows that proximity to Christ is no substitute for surrender to him — the warning every apostle, and every Christian, must hear.
